item.title: ‘Out in Public View’: Indian Americans Say Racism Is Front and Center
item.description:
For months, many Indian Americans said that they had noticed what seemed to be a marked uptick in racist comments against South Asians in some corners of social media.

But two recent incidents have left some in the community wondering whether the anti-South Asian hate that they thought was a fringe sentiment was perhaps not so fringe after all.

As part of the rollout of a new tip line to report truckers suspected of fraud, the Department of Homeland Security posted an image on Sept. 9 of a “Transformers” character facing off with a Sikh man, along with the words: “America for Americans. Get off our roads. You don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” Singh is a common surname for followers of the Sikh faith.

A few days later, Bo French, a Republican candidate for statewide office in Texas, posted an image from a University of Texas football game showing cheering students who appeared to be of South Asian heritage. He wrote: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

For many, the posts confirmed an uneasy sense that the immigration debate has led to rising animus against people of South Asian descent and that it has crept into mainstream American politics, particularly on the right.

“What we’re seeing now is full blown and out in public view,” said Manjusha Kulkarni, co-director of Stop AAPI Hate, a nonprofit that tracks discrimination against Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders. “When agency officials and candidates use this language, it gets weaponized and utilized by those who are perpetrating hate.”

There was backlash to the posts and some backtracking. Mr. French later said that his post was “not about race, it’s about policy,” specifically what he believed to be an admissions policy that favored international students over Americans. (By state law, 90 percent of first-year students at the University of Texas at Austin must be in-state residents.) Mr. French did not respond to a request for comment.

The Department of Homeland Security said that its post was a depiction of Harjinder Singh, an Indian citizen accused of causing a high-profile fatal crash in Florida last year. It later removed the image without explanation.

A few days later, on Sept. 13, a Sikh trucker named Gurvinder Singh was stabbed 17 times at a Wyoming rest stop. Many Sikh Americans couldn’t help but draw a connection to the heightened rhetoric.

“Before, nobody cared about your race, nobody cared about your color, but now it’s a problem,” said Harinder Singh Dhanoa, 71, a Sikh American trucker based in Sacramento who has been driving trucks for more than 40 years. “They look at you different.”

In a statement, the Homeland Security Department said that any attempt to blame the agency for the Wyoming attack was “RECKLESS” and “FALSE.” It called criticism of its deleted post “nonsensical drivel.”

While the stabbing may have been a rare episode, it fueled fear, leaving many South Asians wondering about their place in the United States.

They are not alone. The Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement has hit the Latino community especially hard. Rhetorical attacks on Muslims by some Texas officials have recently surged.

For some people who trace their heritage to South Asia — which includes India, Pakistan and Bangladesh — the rhetoric has been surprising, in part because many had embraced the stereotype, however problematic, of their community as a “model minority.”

Indian Americans are among the wealthiest demographic groups in America, the most highly educated and the most civically engaged, according to AAPI Data, which collects statistics about Asian Americans. While they make up only 1.5 percent of the country’s population, they are one of the fastest-growing ethnic groups and have become increasingly visible in pop culture, business and politics. Prominent Trump administration figures of Indian descent include Kash Patel, Harmeet Dhillon and Usha Vance.

But lately, some South Asians have found themselves wondering whether that success is now a double-edged sword, especially when economic anxieties are high.

Vivek Ramaswamy, the Trump-endorsed tech entrepreneur running to become Ohio’s first governor of Indian descent, addressed the concerns in an opinion article last year. Criticizing the rising vision of American identity based on heritage, he said, “My social media feeds are littered with hundreds of slurs, most from accounts that I don’t recognize.”

For many South Asians, the concerns have intensified as the Trump administration has sought to restrict legal and illegal immigration, and federal and some Republican state officials have repeatedly accused immigrants of taking jobs from Americans.

A dominant theme in the recent surge in online hate speech has been the xenophobic narrative of an Indian “invasion” or “great replacement,” according to a recent report from Stop AAPI Hate.

“It feels like everybody is looking at Asian Indians now with a little bit of skepticism,” said Shiva Peram, 52, a naturalized American citizen who immigrated in 1997 from India.

Mr. Peram moved to Frisco, Texas, about a decade ago, drawn by the warm weather and the top schools for his two sons. He felt safe in the Dallas suburb and voted for President Trump twice because of concerns about illegal immigration, part of a recent rightward shift among Indian Americans, who mostly vote Democratic.

That began to change late last year when Frisco, with a fast-growing South Asian population, became the epicenter of a right-wing furor over H-1B visas, a skilled worker program. In 2023, around three-quarters of the 400,000 or so approved H-1B applications were for workers from India, according to Pew Research Center.

Since then, Mr. Peram said he often found himself overthinking everything. Were people at Costco smiling less at him? When the Caucasian teenagers harassed him and his friends at the volleyball court, were they acting out of racism or were they just acting like kids?

“It’s always in my subconscious,” Mr. Peram said.

Beyond Frisco, some people of South Asian descent said they had heard about growing racism but had not felt an impact in their daily lives.

“I have not seen it become more prevalent,” said Satinder Bharaj, 61, a Sikh American and longtime resident of Ohio.

To some, the animus felt worse after the Sept. 11 attacks, when many South Asians — particularly Sikhs, whose turbans are a visible marker of their faith — were the target of widespread racial profiling and hate attacks.

But Pawan Dhingra, an American studies professor at Amherst College, said that in some ways, events today were more troubling. After Sept. 11, Mr. Dhingra said, the primary concern was about terrorist threats and loyalty to the country. Many Arab Americans and South Asian Americans could respond by flying the American flag and denouncing terrorism.

But Mr. French’s University of Texas post, he noted, attacked students who were celebrating their team’s victory while wearing school colors and cowboy hats. What could be more American — and Texan — than that?

Some people, he said, are worried about a threat to their overall culture and their way of life.

“That is a much deeper fear,” he said. “You can’t wear or say anything that’s going to mitigate that fear.”

Rahul Kodali, a senior majoring in computer science, was one of those students wearing a cowboy hat whom Mr. French later referred to as “foreigners.” Mr. Kodali was born in Syracuse, N.Y., and grew up in Flower Mound, a suburb of Dallas.

In an interview, Mr. Kodali said international students were not a “problem,” emphasizing that most people he knew had come legally and worked hard.

Mr. Kodali said he had not experienced any racial discrimination before this incident and seemed equally at ease talking about his love of the Dallas Cowboys and his favorite childhood Indian meals.

But after Mr. French’s post, he said that he had to reassure his mother that she should not regret her decision to raise her children in the United States.

“I told her, ‘I never feel that way, so don’t ever worry about that,’” he recalled.

For many Sikh truckers, the recent events have felt personal.

Some Sikh truckers said that while they supported boosting safety measures in the industry, the Trump administration was embracing policies that disproportionately affected immigrant truckers, like a rule that limits certain immigrants from obtaining truck driver’s licenses. They worry that the Homeland Security Department’s new fraud tip line could encourage racial profiling.

And, they say, the administration seems to be seizing on fatal accidents involving immigrant drivers as pretext to further crack down.

Now there are also fears about physical safety. After Mr. Singh, the Sikh truck driver, was stabbed at a rest area near Rock Springs, Wyo., the police arrested a man but they have not disclosed a motive. The county sheriff’s office declined to discuss the case, citing its ongoing investigation.

In a phone interview last week, from the hospital where he was recovering, the driver said that he did not know why he was attacked. But he wonders whether the Homeland Security Department’s recent post — “You can’t drive Mr. Singh” — may have played a role.

“What is being built up in people’s hearts,” Mr. Singh asked, “that they would want to do something so terrible to another human being?”

item.title: Democrats Show Strength in Michigan Senate Race but Trail in Maine, Polls Find
item.description:
Democrats appear to be holding off Republican attempts to flip Senate seats in Michigan and New Hampshire but are struggling in their efforts to oust a Republican in Maine, according to New York Times/Siena University polls of three battlegrounds.

In Michigan, the party’s nominee, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, has consolidated Democratic support despite worries about party unity after a divisive primary race. He leads his Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers, by five percentage points.

In New Hampshire, the Democratic nominee, Representative Chris Pappas, is running five points ahead of his Republican rival, former Senator John E. Sununu. The result could dampen Republican hopes that the state might be more competitive than expected.

But in Maine, Senator Susan Collins, who has been seen as her party’s most vulnerable incumbent, holds an edge of three points over Troy Jackson, her Democratic challenger. Her showing, which comes after a sudden switch of the Democratic nominee, could fuel Democratic worries that they will again lose to Ms. Collins in the light-blue state.

[Follow all of the latest polls heading into November’s elections.]

The results underscore the uncertainty both parties are confronting in a series of tight Senate contests. While Republicans are navigating an increasingly grim national political environment, Democrats face a challenge in winning races against well-established G.O.P. politicians with long histories of serving their states.

To win control of the Senate, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats, including some in states President Trump won by double digits, and keep all of their own. Maine was widely considered Democrats’ best chance of defeating an incumbent Republican, but their prospects were scrambled after the summer implosion of Graham Platner’s campaign and Mr. Jackson’s quick ascent.

The survey is the worst result for Mr. Jackson in any public poll since he earned the nomination in July.

Likely voters, Aug. 31–Sept. 6

Note: Margins are calculated using unrounded vote shares when available.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

The poll was conducted almost entirely before ProPublica published a report on Tuesday detailing how the F.B.I. in 2025 shut down an inquiry into allegations that a top ally of Ms. Collins’s had participated in a scheme to funnel illegal campaign contributions from a defense contractor. A Collins spokeswoman vigorously denied the allegations.

The poll found that independent voters, a crucial group, were deeply divided over whom to support in the three states. In both Michigan and Maine, independents were nearly evenly split between Democrats and Republicans. In New Hampshire, the group leaned toward supporting Mr. Pappas, the Democrat, by 10 points.

In all three states, the Democratic candidates are being lifted by a broad dislike of Mr. Trump and his policies. A majority of voters disapproved of his handling of a series of top issues, including immigration, tariffs, the war with Iran, the cost of living and gas prices. Nearly two-thirds of voters described the president as generally focused on the wrong issues.

“I hate to be so partisan, but my feelings right now are there are no Republicans that are willing to stand up to Trump,” said Scott Grady, an independent from Hillsborough, N.H., who is supporting Mr. Pappas. “That’s forcing me to not even look at the Republican side of the ticket and just want to vote straight Democratic.”

Yet across all three states, the Republican nominees for Senate outperformed Mr. Trump’s 35 percent approval rating, sometimes by double digits. Their stronger standing signals that some G.O.P. candidates might be able to overcome the drag that the unpopular president is causing on his party.

While a majority of voters in these states view the Republican Party as too far to the right, most voters do not see the G.O.P. candidates in their states as too extreme.

And in all three states, support for the individual Democratic candidates falls short of a general desire for the party to win power in Congress. Overall, 54 percent of voters said they would prefer Democrats to control the Senate, a greater share than the percentage supporting any of the three candidates.

In Maine, 12 percent of voters who said they preferred Democrats to control the Senate also said they planned to support Ms. Collins — a split that helped explain her lead.

Views of Ms. Collins have warmed slightly since June, when she was narrowly underwater with voters in the last Times/Siena poll of Maine. Now a majority — 51 percent — view her positively, including nearly half of independent voters.

Ms. Collins is also seen by a majority of Maine voters as more likely than Mr. Jackson to be an effective senator and as having better character. By contrast, Mr. Jackson is viewed more unfavorably than favorably.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Sept. 15-22

Based on a New York Times/Siena/Portland Press Herald poll of 619 voters in Maine and on New York Times/Siena polls of 605 voters in Michigan and 613 voters in New Hampshire. Net favorability is the share of respondents who view the candidate favorably minus the share who view the candidate unfavorably.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

The survey shows that voters tend to agree with what Ms. Collins has pitched as her strongest selling point: that she delivers for the state. By a wide margin, voters were more likely to see her as better at bringing money and resources to Maine as they were to say the same of Mr. Jackson.

Ms. Collins still faces headwinds in the state, though. A majority of Mainers, including a majority of independents and 12 percent of Republicans, said they preferred a candidate who would provide a check on Mr. Trump.

Claude Junkins, a Republican in Holden, Maine, said he planned to support Ms. Collins despite her support of Mr. Trump.

“Sometimes she does go with some of Trump’s crazy ideas, and you’ve got to wonder sometimes what she’s thinking,” said Mr. Junkins, 70, a retired facilities director.

But he added: “She works for Maine. If it’s got anything to do with Maine, she’s going to fight for us.”

In Michigan, support for Dr. El-Sayed appears to be fueled by the popularity of his economic message and his vocal support for single-payer health care. He is more trusted to handle the cost of living by nine points, the only Democrat who is more trusted on the issue across the three states. And despite a bitter primary, a whopping 95 percent of Democrats are now supporting his candidacy.

Dr. El-Sayed is also winning 8 percent of voters who supported Mr. Trump in the 2024 election, more than either of the other two Democrats in the survey.

Abel Kang, a social worker from Grand Rapids, said he knew very little about Mr. Rogers other than his support of Mr. Trump. Mr. Kang said he planned to support Dr. El-Sayed largely because of economic issues and his support of single-payer health care.

“He is talking about free health care,” said Mr. Kang, 47, an independent. “Personally, I think that is a necessity. It’s a basic human need.”

The New York Times/Siena Poll

Sept. 15-22

Based on a New York Times/Siena/Portland Press Herald poll of 619 voters in Maine and on New York Times/Siena polls of 605 voters in Michigan and 613 voters in New Hampshire.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

In all three Senate races, economic worries far outpace concerns about foreign policy — either the war with Iran or the situation in Israel and Gaza. Thirty-six percent said economic concerns, including jobs, inflation and the cost of living, were the most important issue deciding their vote, while only eight percent named foreign policy.

Concerns about foreign policy were more pronounced in New Hampshire and Michigan, where debates over Israel have raged in both the Democratic primary and the general election.

Voters in Michigan were divided over which candidate they trusted to best handle foreign wars: 46 percent preferred Dr. El-Sayed, while 43 percent preferred Mr. Rogers.

“I trust him zero percent,” Sandra Campbell, a self-described moderate conservative from Macomb county, said of Dr. El-Sayed. “I think that he would lean more toward foreign policy that would be anti-American.”

In recent weeks, Republicans have grown more hopeful of pulling off an upset in New Hampshire, which is seen as competitive despite not electing a Republican to the Senate since 2010. But the poll indicates that Mr. Pappas has a comfortable lead.

Still, even in New Hampshire, views of the Democratic Party brand remain dim, with majorities saying Democrats are divided and generally focused on the wrong issues.

Across all three states, 44 percent of Democrats said they identified as “democratic socialist,” while 50 percent said they did not. Just 21 percent of Democrats viewed socialism unfavorably.

“The Democrats need to get a message,” said Laura Platt-Lunardo, an independent from Exeter, N.H., who is supporting Mr. Pappas. “And they need to get some core things down, like this is what we’re actually going to do and this is how we’re going to do it.”

item.title: Abortion Pills, Vaccines and Food Safety: F.D.A. Nominee to Face Senate Panel
item.description:
President Trump’s nominee to run the Food and Drug Administration is expected to be closely questioned in her Senate confirmation hearing on Thursday about her views on abortion pills, vaccines and highly contested products under F.D.A. review that include A.I. tools and peptide injections.

Dr. Heidi Overton, the nominee, is a top domestic policy adviser at the White House and a former chief policy adviser at a conservative think tank. Her background is far more political than that of previous F.D.A. leaders. She has been a loyal foot soldier to Mr. Trump and Susie Wiles, his chief of staff, according to people familiar with the dynamics who were not authorized to speak publicly.

She would be the first F.D.A. commissioner who has openly opposed use of mifepristone, an abortion pill currently under a safety review by the agency following a push from anti-abortion groups. She has called the drug “dangerous to women” and described the 2022 Supreme Court ruling overturning Roe v. Wade as “a huge victory for life.”

Last month, Dr. Overton stood by Mr. Trump as he signed an executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccinations. She was also a key driver of a plan for federal officials to stop recommending vaccines that protect children from the flu, RSV and meningitis.

The job of running the F.D.A. has always been subject to immense pressure, given billions of dollars that hang in the balance from agency’s regulatory decisions. That pressure has grown during Mr. Trump’s second term, as the administration has forged alliances with backers of tobacco products, artificial intelligence software, cannabis and hemp products, peptides, and an addictive gas-station drug called kratom.

“I think this is a key moment for the integrity of the F.D.A.,” said Dr. Joshua Sharfstein, a former principal deputy commissioner of the F.D.A. and pediatrician. “People are looking to the agency not just because of who is in a particular position, but because of the way the agency does its work. That’s what gives it credibility, and so if that is overridden again and again, then people wonder whether the F.D.A. has integrity in its positions.”

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Dr. Overton’s nomination comes amid efforts by abortion opponents and lawsuits filed by conservative states to press the F.D.A. to roll back access to mifepristone. As a result of such dynamics, the F.D.A. has begun its safety review, and a looming test for the agency will be any decisions it makes after concluding that review.

Mifepristone, which was approved by the F.D.A. in 2000, is the first pill taken in the typical two-drug medication abortion regimen. That is now the most common method of terminating pregnancies in the United States.

More than 100 studies have found that mifepristone is safe and that serious complications from taking it are rare. Last fall, under the Trump administration, the F.D.A. granted approval for a new generic version of the medication.

Dr. Overton was the co-author of a 2023 think tank paper that criticized the F.D.A.’s decisions, beginning in 2021, to broaden the availability of abortion pills, especially by removing a requirement that patients obtain mifepristone in person from a medical provider. That decision allowed mifepristone to be prescribed through telemedicine and sent by mail, which has become a major way patients get access to the medication. She has referred to medication abortion as “chemical abortion,” a term frequently used by anti-abortion activists.

“Abortion is corrosive to children, women and society broadly because it devalues and extinguishes innocent human life,” Dr. Overton and her co-author wrote. “Unfortunately, federal policymakers have recently expanded access to abortion pills, also called chemical abortions, which are far more dangerous to women, enabling rapid access to abortion.”

Vaccines are likely to be another flashpoint.

Dr. Overton, who has a medical degree and a doctorate in clinical investigation, played key roles developing administration policies that many public health experts say have eroded trust in vaccines.

She worked on an effort to upend longstanding advice from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, eliminating recommendations for children receive vaccinations for flu, RSV, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, hepatitis A and hepatitis B.

The change has been blocked by a court for now, but Dr. Overton described a presidential executive order issued in August as a way to encourage states to adopt the pared-down recommendations anyway.

If confirmed, Dr. Overton would lead the agency through a number of high-profile decisions and initiatives on other issues across the agency’s vast portfolio, including medications, food, tobacco and medical devices, which include diagnostics and A.I. software.

Lawmakers have been particularly interested in the agency’s recent changes in tobacco policy, which have followed large donations from the industry and included new authorizations of flavored e-cigarettes. The topic was contentious within the administration and led to the resignation of Dr. Marty Makary, the former commissioner.

The agency is also in the process of discussing how it might regulate advanced artificial intelligence tools such agentic A.I., which can perform tasks of physicians like prescribing medications. Given the lack of rules applicable to newer A.I. models, the agency is allowing some A.I. pilots to go forward without agency authorization. One enables an A.I. chatbot to provide therapy to Medicare patients with anxiety or depression.

Early next year, the F.D.A. will also reconvene a panel to determine whether untested and unproven peptide injections should be added to a list of substances that are allowed to be dispensed by specialized pharmacies.

Telehealth companies, including Hims & Hers and Noom, sent representatives to a recent hearing who expressed interest in selling the substances, which are popular among social media influencers. Such sales could expose a wide swath of the public to products with little safety testing. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said he would like to see them made widely available.

Food safety has also become a pressing topic. Over the summer, an outbreak of food-borne illnesses from the cyclospora parasite on lettuce sickened thousands. F.D.A. officials are working on reports about their investigation of a Taylor Farms processing center in Mexico tied to the outbreak.

The agency has also moved forward with a proposed rule to close a loophole that allows companies to introduce new chemicals in food with no notice to the agency. The proposal allows companies to avoid detailed reporting requirements during an initial 45-day period after it is finalized and also if they claim that the ingredient is consumed in minimal amounts across a typical diet.

Those exemptions render the rule nearly meaningless, said Scott Faber, senior vice president of government affairs for the Environmental Working Group. He said Dr. Overton, if confirmed, should tear up the proposal and write a stronger one.

“Food safety is a kitchen table issue,” he said, “and consumers are more concerned than in any time in my career that the food they’re eating may make them sick either right away or years from now.”

item.title: ‘Survival Mode Time’: Republicans Accelerate Their Break With Trump
item.description:
Forty days before the midterm elections, a growing number of Republican candidates across the country are openly seeking to distance themselves from President Trump, breaking with a leader who has long held an iron grip on his party.

On Monday, the Republicans running for Senate in both Michigan and Iowa called on the president to end the war in Iran as a way to reverse the escalating price of gas. On Tuesday, G.O.P. candidates for governor in Wisconsin and Michigan, along with an embattled Republican senator in Ohio, followed.

“The war with Iran needs to end — and end quickly,” former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, said in a video filmed in a grocery store. “When it does, energy costs will plummet.”

On Capitol Hill, three other Republican senators called for an investigation into the president’s son over his lavish wedding after-party paid for by a Russian businessman with ties to President Vladimir V. Putin.

And in Florida, one of Mr. Trump’s close allies, Representative Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor, recently overhauled his website to make Mr. Trump’s endorsement far less prominent.

The dissent reflects growing unease about the party’s prospects in November, as Republicans struggle to overcome the unpopularity of the president and his signature policies.

Mr. Trump’s approval rating is languishing near record lows. On issues where he once was strong — like the economy, national security and immigration — he is now underwater. His approval rating on the economy hit an all-time low of 27 percent, according to a CNN poll released on Tuesday.

“It’s ‘Not great, Bob!’, as they say on Mad Men,” said Nachama Soloveichik, a Republican political strategist, of the darkening political environment for Republicans. “Trump’s approval numbers are down. That’s not good. They’re making strategic decisions based on polling numbers — that’s what happens in political races.”

A White House aide disputed the idea that there is any distance between the president and his party, passing along statements and photos from more than 60 Republican candidates praising and appearing alongside the president.

“President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, in a statement.

There’s a long tradition in American politics of vulnerable candidates running away from unpopular, second-term presidents in midterm elections.

In 2006, a midterm cycle that Democrats often compare to this one, Republicans distanced themselves from President George W. Bush amid backlash to the war in Iraq. Eight years later, Democrats running in red states criticized President Barack Obama, even skirting questions about whether they had voted for him.

But for Mr. Trump, the experience of Republicans publicly criticizing his agenda — and, perhaps most notably, targeting his family — is relatively new. The breadth of Republican opposition will be tested this week, when the Senate votes again on a Democratic-led war powers resolution.

Marc Short, who served as the White House legislative affairs director in Mr. Trump’s first term, said the distancing by Republican candidates in the final weeks of the midterm elections is more pronounced than what happened in 2018 and “does feel somewhat like desperation.”

“If you’ve been carrying the president’s water on all his legislation priorities and his issues, it’s hard now to distance yourself,” said Mr. Short, who also served as former Vice President Mike Pence’s chief of staff. “It appears now as if it’s just for political convenience.”

After facing the indignities of two years in Washington with virtually no power, Democrats can barely contain their glee.

“For the last 10 years, Republicans have been more afraid of Donald Trump than they have the voters they’re supposed to represent,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader, said in an interview. “It’s clear that Republicans are in full panic mode, because Donald Trump’s approval ratings are at extinction levels.”

In past elections, Republicans have struggled to turn out their base when Mr. Trump was not on the ticket. Now, the president and his aides are focused on motivating his most loyal supporters

by working to center the midterms around Mr. Trump himself. This month, he hosted a splashy gathering for his supporters in Dallas, where he spoke for nearly two hours.

“Pretend that I’m on the ballot,” Mr. Trump begged his supporters. “I’m on the ballot. I’m on. Just one more time.”

But at least a few candidates are trying to pretend he’s not even in the White House. Some vulnerable Republicans skipped the event in Dallas, a step widely interpreted as an effort to put distance between their campaigns and the unpopular president.

Many of those who attended offered a quick mention of the Trump administration’s policies before turning their focus on castigating their Democratic opponents as communist, socialist and un-American.

“The Republicans might be a little bit astray but the Democrats have lost their minds,” said John Catsimatidis, a New York based Republican donor, who hosted a fund-raiser last week for around 10 Senate Republicans.

“I think the American people may not like some of the things the president has been doing,” he acknowledged, before adding, “I support the president 110 percent.”

In the past, breaking with Mr. Trump has ended the careers of many Republicans, who lost primaries or retired from office to avoid an electoral defeat. The trend continued into this cycle, when Mr. Trump successfully backed challengers to Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, among others.

The decision now to openly criticize signature policies like the Iran war reflects the deep political peril perceived by many in the party.

“The president’s greatest power is his influence in Republican primaries and now all the primaries are behind him,” said Carlos Curbelo, a former Republican congressman from Miami who lost his seat in 2018. “This is survival mode time for Republicans.”

Last week, Representative María Elvira Salazar of Florida — who represents a district Mr. Trump won with 57 percent of the vote — released an ad breaking with Mr. Trump on immigration. It was seen as a sign both of Mr. Trump’s collapsing support in Hispanic communities and the degree to which districts he carried by 10 percentage points or more in 2024 have become swing districts in 2026.

Mr. Trump has sometimes cracked down on dissidents in his party. But on Friday the president said that while he “disagreed” with Ms. Salazar, he was not pulling his support — and took credit for her past victories.

Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, whose re-election is getting fresh attention, also seemed to raise questions of the Trump administration’s immigration operations on Wednesday. “When ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement,” he wrote on X.

But Democrats say escaping the president’s pull may be difficult for candidates who marched in lock step with him for nearly a decade. Many are now running ads linking their Republican opponents directly to the president.

“He votes 100 percent for Trump,” Manny Rutinel, a Democrat running for Congress in Colorado, says of Representative Gabe Evans, the Republican incumbent, in one ad.

In Iowa, the decision by Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate candidate, to declare that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end” brought guffaws from Democrats who noted that she had voted multiple times — including last week — against a war powers resolution that would have constrained the president.

Two other Iowa Republicans running in swing districts — Representatives Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks — recently reversed their previous positions to help push through a Democratic measure directing Mr. Trump to halt the conflict.

Iowa, in some ways, is at the center of the pushback against the president as the state grapples with the impact of both tariffs and higher fuel costs. Senator Chuck Grassley, Republican of Iowa, delivered a speech on the Senate floor on Tuesday calling for a temporary embargo on diesel exports to drive down prices.

Senator Dan Sullivan, Republican of Alaska, who is facing a tough re-election fight, echoed Mr. Grassley’s call.

“The cost of diesel is just too damn high,” said Mr. Sullivan, long a staunch ally of the president, in a statement.

A day after Mr. Trump told reporters he was considering the idea, his energy secretary, Chris Wright, dismissed it.

“Nobody wants a full blanket ban or zero exports of diesel,” Mr. Wright said at the Climate Forward live event in Manhattan. “That’s not being discussed.”

The movement away from Mr. Trump has stretched into some of the most consistently Republican states in the country, where Republican candidates are trying to walk a careful line between distancing themselves from the president without alienating his supporters.

In Florida, the changes to Mr. Donald’s website — which included removing a “Trump-Endorsed” box at the top, a yellow banner featuring the endorsement and a photo depicting the president, Mr. Donalds and his wife — were notable coming from such an staunch Trump ally.

Gates McGavick, a spokesman for Mr. Donalds, said the congressman was “proud” to have Mr. Trump’s endorsement and disputed that there was meaning to be drawn from his revamped website, which was first reported by the Miami Herald. “Our campaign website reflects Byron’s focus on the issues that matter most to Floridians — affordability, insurance costs, and government transparency,” he said. “This angle of reporting is FAKE NEWS.”

In Texas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, the leading super PAC helping Senate Republicans this week reserved another $35 million to help lift Ken Paxton, the state attorney general who toppled Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary, over James Talarico, the Democratic nominee.

Mr. Cornyn, meanwhile, joined Senator Thom Tillis, the retiring senator from North Carolina, in backing a call from Senator John Curtis of Utah to subpoena the president’s son, saying he would support an investigation by the Judiciary Committee, of which he is still a senior member.

item.title: American Bar Association Fights to Keep Power to Vet Law Schools
item.description:
The American Bar Association is on the precipice of losing its power to accredit law schools as a federal panel weighs whether to recommend the punitive measure to the Education Department.

The vote was scheduled for Wednesday, but the deadlocked panel — known as the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity — delayed its decision until Thursday. It was unclear how the panel would resolve its differences.

The panel’s longtime members and staff said they could not recall when the group had failed to reach a majority decision on a recommendation. The panel’s 18 members are appointed by the secretary of education, the Senate president and the House speaker, with several appointees recommended by minority party lawmakers.

“Hopefully we can find a creative solution,” said Jay P. Greene, the chairman of the advisory panel and research director at Do No Harm, a group that campaigns against diversity, equity and inclusion programs and youth gender-affirming care in medicine.

Officials from the bar association’s accreditation agency, known as the Council of the ABA Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar, declined to comment after the meeting.

A report earlier this month by staff of the Education Department urged the panel to recommend stripping the accreditation role from the bar association, the nation’s largest organization of lawyers. Such a move would strike a blow to a group that has battled the Trump administration over its attacks on law firms and also open a front in the administration’s pressure campaign on higher education.

The panel’s recommendation would be sent to Nicholas Kent, the No. 2 official at the Education Department, who has been a key enforcer of the administration’s bid to reshape academia. Mr. Kent would have 90 days to decide whether to oust the bar association from its perch as the nation’s gatekeeper of legal education, which it has held for the past five decades.

If the bar association loses its vetting powers, law schools would have to cobble together different forms of accreditation. Accreditation is required under federal law for students to have access to billions in federal aid, including work-study programs and student loans available to law students.

Law schools attached to universities could rely on their school’s institutional accrediting body. Education Department officials said about a half-dozen stand-alone, independent law schools do not have accreditation from regional bodies, but expected those schools to find other accreditation.

The bigger blow appeared to be aimed at the bar association. Founded in Chicago nearly 150 years ago, the group has been fighting with the federal government since last year, when it sued to stop the Trump administration from punishing law firms it did not like.

The bar association, which has locked horns with the Education Department and the advisory panel multiple times in the past 20 years, tried to curry favor with the Trump administration earlier this month by repealing its diversity requirement for law schools. The bar association, which oversees about 200 juris doctorate programs in the country, said the requirement was a risk to its accreditation role.

But whether that concession would be enough to save its accreditation powers remained unclear. Bar association officials on Wednesday maintained that they were in compliance with federal regulations.

“We think we have the right focus,” said Daniel Thies, who until recently was the chair of the bar association’s accreditation agency. “We are focused on our students. We are focused on the legal system. We’re focused on making sure lawyers are qualified.”

Half of the panel was in favor of extending time to the bar association on compliance issues.

“I’m really struggling to see what the big harm is right now to students from the American Bar Association,” said Zakiya Smith Ellis, a former New Jersey secretary of education, who supported giving more time to the bar association.

But other members of the advisory panel said they were uncomfortable with what they viewed as too cozy of a relationship between the bar association’s accreditation body and the association itself.

Arthur Keiser, an advisory panel member who manages the operations of about two dozen Keiser University campuses in Florida and abroad, said the association’s accreditation body had a history of noncompliance with federal standards. He supported stripping the group’s power.

“They have been out of compliance for a long time,” Mr. Keiser said. “I don’t feel sorry for them.”
